training set.simple: The part of the data a model learns from. In time series it is the older part.

test set.simple: The part of the data kept hidden to measure how good the model is. In time series it is the newest part.

cutoff.simple: The date that separates training data from test data.
cutoff.example: Cutoff 2024-03-01: all rows before it are training rows.

embargo.simple: A gap of skipped rows between train and test so that overlapping features or labels cannot leak across the cutoff.
embargo.example: A 7-day sum label needs an embargo of 7 days.

backtest.simple: Testing a forecasting method on the past by pretending to forecast from several earlier dates and comparing with what really happened.
backtest.example: Forecast 14 days ahead from 12 different weekly origins.

forecast origin.simple: The last date that is known when a forecast is made. Data after it is hidden from the model.
forecast origin.example: Origin = day 100: you train with days 1 to 100.

horizon.simple: How many steps ahead a forecast looks.
horizon.example: Horizon 7 on daily data means the next 7 days.

mae.simple: Mean absolute error: the average size of the errors, ignoring their sign.

rmse.simple: Root mean squared error: square the errors, average, take the square root. Big errors count more.

quantile.simple: A cut point of a distribution. The 0.9 quantile has 90% of the outcomes below it.
quantile.example: P50 is the median; P90 is the 0.9 quantile.

pinball loss.simple: A score for a quantile forecast. It punishes under- and over-forecasts with different weights, tau and 1 - tau.
pinball loss.example: tau = 0.9, forecast 10 too low: loss 9. Forecast 10 too high: loss 1.

prediction interval.simple: A range that should contain the future value with a stated probability, such as 80%.
prediction interval.example: The 80% interval for tomorrow is 90 to 115.

calibration.simple: How well the stated probabilities match reality. 80% intervals are calibrated if they contain the actual value about 80% of the time.
calibration.example: A 90% interval that covers only 70% of actuals is overconfident.

naive forecast.simple: A forecast that repeats the last known value.

seasonal naive.simple: A forecast that repeats the value from the same point of the last season.
seasonal naive.example: Daily data, season 7: tomorrow equals the value 7 days ago.

look-ahead bias.simple: A mistake where the model uses information from after the time of the prediction.
look-ahead bias.example: Using next week's average to predict tomorrow.

standardization.simple: Turning values into z = (x - mean) / sd, so the training data has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
standardization.example: Train mean 50, sd 10: the value 80 becomes 3.

expanding window.simple: A backtest style where the training data grows: it always starts at the first point and ends at the forecast origin.
expanding window.example: Fold 1 trains on days 1-20, fold 2 on days 1-24.

walk-forward validation.simple: A backtest that moves the forecast origin forward step by step and repeats train, forecast, compare.
walk-forward validation.example: Move the origin by 7 days each time.

fold.simple: One round of a backtest: one train part and one test part.
fold.example: Fold 2 trains on days 1-24 and tests on days 25-28.

mape.simple: Mean absolute percentage error: the average of |error| / |actual|, in percent. It breaks when actual is 0.

smape.simple: Symmetric MAPE: the average of 2|error| / (|actual| + |forecast|), in percent.

wape.simple: Weighted absolute percentage error: total absolute error divided by total actual value.

mase.simple: Mean absolute scaled error: your MAE divided by the MAE of the naive method on the training data. Below 1 is better than naive.
mase.example: MASE 0.8 means 20% less error than naive.

rmsse.simple: Root mean squared scaled error: like MASE, but for squared errors. Used in the M5 competition.
rmsse.example: RMSSE 1.2 means worse than the naive method.

coverage.simple: The share of actual values that fall inside the prediction interval.

interval score.simple: A score for an interval: its width plus a penalty for each actual outside it. Lower is better (also called Winkler score).

crps.simple: Continuous ranked probability score: one number for a whole forecast distribution. It is the pinball loss averaged over all quantile levels (times 2).
crps.example: For a single-value forecast, CRPS equals the absolute error.

sharpness.simple: How narrow the prediction intervals are. Narrow is good, but only if the intervals are calibrated.
sharpness.example: An 80% interval of width 10 is sharper than one of width 40.

conformal prediction.simple: A method that builds prediction intervals from past errors of any model, with almost no assumptions about the error shape.
conformal prediction.example: Use the 8th smallest of 9 calibration errors as half-width.

calibration set.simple: Data the model did not train on, used to measure its errors so that interval widths can be set.
calibration set.example: The last 60 days before the test period.

exchangeable.simple: Data points are exchangeable if their order does not matter, as if drawn from the same process.
exchangeable.example: Shuffled coin flips are exchangeable; a trending series is not.

rolling-window conformal.simple: Conformal prediction that uses only the last W known residuals for each new interval, so it can follow changes.

adaptive conformal inference.simple: A conformal method that changes its target miss rate after each step: a miss makes the next interval wider.

enbpi.simple: Ensemble batch prediction intervals: a conformal method for time series that uses an ensemble of models trained on bootstrap samples and updates the residuals over time.
enbpi.example: Used when no separate calibration set is possible.

forecast value added.simple: The accuracy gain of a forecasting method over a simple baseline such as seasonal naive.
forecast value added.example: MAE 8 against baseline MAE 10: a gain of 20%.

average rank.simple: The mean position of a model when the models are ranked on each series (1 is best).
average rank.example: Ranks 1, 2, 1 give an average rank of 1.33.

geometric mean.simple: The n-th root of the product of n numbers. It is the fair average for ratios.
geometric mean.example: The geometric mean of 0.5 and 2 is 1.

diebold-mariano test.simple: A test of whether two forecasts have the same average loss on the same points. It uses the loss difference at each time.
diebold-mariano test.example: A statistic far from 0 (about 2 or more) means the gap is unlikely to be luck.

winner's curse.simple: The best of many tested models has an optimistic score, because selection picks lucky noise.
winner's curse.example: Test 50 models on one period and the best score is too good.
